## TL;DR

I ran a headless QA pass on the Releases publish flow against the built UI, with every `/api` call intercepted, so nothing reached the real release API. Two failure states were genuinely broken and are now fixed: a named blocker such as "v0.7.0 already exists." was invisible in the Cut-a-release drawer while Publish stayed enabled, and a failed CI workflow rendered no alert when the distribution list was empty. I also made the CI alert and the already-exists server message say what to do next. The new browser test file has 8 passing scenarios, and the scoped `repoos check` is green.

## Work and rationale

The task asked for failure and long-content coverage at 375, 768 and 1280 px, with no real release and no visible browser. The shared UI harness already gave me a headless WebKit launcher and a built-app preview server, and `offline-slow-network-browser.test.ts` showed how to stub `/api` with route interception. I followed that pattern.

The stub has two properties I cared about. The catch-all answers 404 and never continues to the server, so a missed stub cannot publish anything. Each scenario counts `POST /api/release` requests, so "nothing is published by accident" is asserted directly.

Reading the publish code before writing tests showed two suspect spots. The Publish button's `:disabled` condition included `canOpen` but not `blockers`, so a named blocker could leave Publish enabled. The "Published to" section was gated on channels, a load, or a refresh error, so a `ciFailure` with an empty channel list rendered nothing. The tests confirmed both: the tag-exists scenario showed no blocker text and an enabled Publish button, and the CI scenario found no `role="alert"` at all. I wrote those two tests before changing the view, so they demonstrate the bugs rather than just passing afterwards.

The fixes are small. The drawer now lists `blockers` under "Publishing is blocked until these are fixed", and both the Publish button's `:disabled` and `release()`'s guard refuse while any blocker is present. `release()` matters because Enter in the version field calls it directly, so the button alone would not stop that path. The distribution section also renders when `distributionCiFailure` is set. The CI alert now says to open the failed run, fix the cause, and re-run the failed jobs, or cut a new version if the fix needs new code. The server's "already exists, so nothing was published" message gained "Pick a new version number and publish again." No existing test pinned that wording.

I added `method()` to the `SmokeRoute.request()` type in `src/commands/ui-harness.ts`. The runtime Playwright object already had it, and the test needs it to tell a GET from a POST. Without the type change, `vue-tsc` rejects the test file, which fails `bun run build:ui`.

I added `data-test-id="release-publish"` to the drawer's Publish button, following its neighbours, so the test can target it without depending on text.

The QA note is at `docs/qa/2026-11-release-flow-failures-qa.md`. It records only what this run observed, lists what was not verified, and includes no screenshots.

## Approaches tried

I first wrote the test with the `SmokePage` helpers `fill`, `locator`, and `waitForSelector`. Those methods are not on the narrow harness type, so `vue-tsc` failed the build. I rewrote it to use `focus`, `click`, `waitForFunction` and `evaluate`, and set field values with the native value setter plus an `input` event, which is what Vue's `v-model` listens for. The Publish button needed a `data-test-id` to be reachable with a stable selector.

For the failed-run scenario I first stubbed the whole API twice and used `unroute` between the stubs. A later `page.route` for `/api/release/run` takes precedence over the catch-all, so one stub is enough.

My first Vitest runs used the wrong runner. Running `bunx vitest run` without the UI config produced `window is not defined` for the shot-preview fixtures and many other files, which looked like 63 regressions. Re-running with `--config src/ui-app/vite.config.ts`, the way `test:vitest` does, gave 16 files and 382 tests passing. I checked this before treating any failure as real.

The UI build initially looked fine but was actually stale. The build failed on the test-file types and left the previous `dist/ui` in place, so my first post-fix run still showed the old behaviour. I caught it by reading the build log's exit code, not by trusting the test output, and rebuilt after the type fix.

## Challenges and blockers

The main constraint was that I could not observe a real release, a real CI run, or a real network outage. The CI-failure and already-exists states are fixture-driven, and the offline case is an aborted request rather than a stopped server. The QA note says so explicitly, and I did not write any claim that those paths were observed.

Notes have no separate save endpoint. The textarea value is sent with the cut. So the acceptance criterion "notes can be edited and saved" can only be checked as the value surviving a failed attempt and a resize, not as a server-side draft. I recorded that gap rather than inventing a save.

The `repoos check` test step was skipped (`REPOOS_SKIP_TESTS=1`, the suite runs on the remote validation runner). I ran the Releases-related UI tests directly, so the scoped check's build, lint, contrast and smoke steps passed, and the tests I touched also passed. The full unscoped suite is still for the merge gate.

## Key learnings

Reading the template gating against the data model found the CI bug faster than the browser did. The alert lived inside a section whose condition ignored it, so no amount of stubbing a CI failure would have shown it unless the stub also had channels. When a message is conditionally rendered, check the condition against every field that message depends on, not only the ones the happy path sets.

A disabled button is not a guard. `release()` is also reached by Enter in the version field, so any blocker check has to live in the function as well as on the button. The test that presses Enter with a blocker present is what proves this.

Failed-state tests need a deliberately non-success stub on each path, and the fallback must never reach the real server. The catch-all returning 404 made any unplanned call visible as a failure rather than a silent real request.

Build exit codes matter more than the test output when a build gates a browser test. A type error in a test file can leave an old bundle in place, and tests run against that bundle look like they are checking the new code.
